study.title: 1 Kings 10 The fame, the riches, and the limits of the glory of Solomon
study.overview: The chapter shows Solomon at the height of his reputation, wealth and international prestige. The queen of Sheba comes to test her wisdom and ends up recognizing that what she heard was true, but even less than reality. Then the text extends the picture with the description of the king's annual income, his utensils, his throne, his fleet and the trade of horses and chariots. The chapter presents Solomon's glory as a result of the wisdom granted by God, but also lets a prosperity be seen so great that it borders excess and ostentation.

outline.title: The Queen of Sheba's Visit and the Confirmation of Solomon's Wisdom
outline.explanation: The queen arrives with great entourage and difficult questions, observes the wisdom, organization of the royal house and the worship of Solomon, and recognizes that reality overcomes fame. His central speech not only praises Solomon, but blesses the Lord, attributing to God the king's choice to practice righteousness. The meeting also involves valuable gifts and seems to have diplomatic and commercial tone, without losing the main focus: God granted wisdom to Solomon.

outline.title: The immense wealth of the king and the signs of royal luxury
outline.explanation: The text lists the annual gold income, taxes and imports, as well as describing shields, smaller shields, a throne of ivory covered in gold and entirely golden utensils. The repetition of precious materials highlights the opulence of the kingdom. The chapter points out that in Solomon's time, silver lost value in the face of the abundance of gold.

outline.title: Solomon as a world reference in wisdom and wealth
outline.explanation: Here the narrator summarizes the height of the reign: Solomon exceeded all kings in wisdom and riches, and peoples of all the earth sought him. The annual tributes and the concentration of cars, knights, silver and cedars reinforce the image of a centralized, admired and very prosperous kingdom. At the same time, the material magnitude occupies the first plane of the description.

outline.title: The trade of horses and chariots between Egypt, Coa and the northern kingdoms
outline.explanation: The text concludes by describing the circulation of horses from Egypt and Coa through the king's merchants. The final verse shows chariots and horses being resold to other kings, including the Hittites and Syrians. Thus, Solomon appears not only as a rich king, but also as a commercial intermediary between different regions.

study.context: The chapter belongs to the period of Israel's united kingdom and depicts Solomon's rule in its most prosperous phase. The account is not only biographical; it also has theological function, showing that the king's fame reaches other nations and that his wisdom comes from God. The notes indicate that the Queen of Sheba probably came from a region south of Canaan, associated with the trade in spices and precious goods, which helps explain the diplomatic and economic nature of the visit.
study.theology: The theology of the chapter emphasizes that wisdom, honor, and authority proceed from the Lord. The queen of Sheba correctly interprets Solomon's ascension as a divine act: God placed him on the throne to exercise law and justice. At the same time, the chapter shows that material prosperity is not an autonomous sign of spiritual approval; it can accompany God's blessing, but also exposes the risk of the king becoming a symbol of excessive magnificence. The text therefore unites blessing, responsibility and discernment: Solomon's greatness exists so that the government reflects the righteousness of God, not just the human splendor.

scholarViews.insight: The visit of the queen of Sheba acts as a test of Solomon's reputation and at the same time as a recognition that his wisdom and possessions come from the wisdom given by God.
The account highlights Solomon's extreme prosperity and the greatness of his kingdom, but material glory does not replace concern for mercy; the chapter itself insists on his public magnificence.
The verse closes the section showing Solomon as a commercial intermediary, with chariots and horses moving from Egypt to other kingdoms through his merchants.

questions: What most draws my attention in this chapter: the wisdom of Solomon, his wealth, or the recognition that everything comes from the LORD?
In what areas my life risks seeking appearance and prestige without the righteousness that God desires?
How can I use resources, influence, and knowledge so that they point to God and not just to me?
study.practice: Examine today whether his admiration for competence, wealth or success is being placed in the place of reverence to God. Apply the text by seeking two concrete attitudes: first, thank God for every gift and opportunity; second, use what you have received to promote justice, integrity and service to others. If you occupy any leadership position, ask God for wisdom to rule, decide and speak so that people see not only efficiency, but also fear of the Lord.
study.uncertainty: The chapter does not directly inform the exact identity of the queen of Sheba or details with absolute precision the geography of Saba, Coa or Tarshish; therefore, these points must be treated with caution and only according to the indications of the notes. Nor can one claim, from this chapter alone, the final judgment of God over the whole career of Solomon, only the picture of his glory and prosperity in this stage of the reign.
